name: EJ 01 — The entrepreneur's mindset
description: Part: Foundations. Success in a startup comes from two habits: run the business as efficiently as possible, and beat competitors by being better and different. This module explains why new businesses fail and how to think like a founder who survives.

payload.html: Success in a startup comes from two habits: run the business as efficiently as possible, and beat competitors by being better and different. This module explains why new businesses fail and how to think like a founder who survives.

lessons.name: Why startups fail & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Why startups fail; Small business versus entrepreneurial business; The business life cycle; The three pillars of success; A simple route to opportunity; Proactive versus reactive decisions

payload.html:
Why startups fail

Common causes are running out of cash, weak marketing, too little starting capital, poor pricing, and gaps in the founder's knowledge. When a business fails, the damage spreads: suppliers go unpaid, customers lose deposits, staff lose jobs.

Small business versus entrepreneurial business

A small business is independently owned, run for profit and not dominant in its market. An entrepreneurial business does something different, not just something better. A new café in a busy street is a small business. A café that rethinks how coffee is ordered and delivered is entrepreneurial. You can start as one and become the other.

The business life cycle

Every business moves through predictable stages, and each needs different priorities: 1. Formation: turning an idea into a viable business, raising capital and launching. Priority: validate demand before spending heavily. 2. Early growth: the business is trading but its future is uncertain. Priority: cash flow, performance and a basic structure. 3. Established: revenue starts to level off and competition increases. Priority: decide whether to consolidate or expand, and put proper controls in place. 4. Mature: the business is stable and efficient. Priority: protect market position and keep innovating.

The three pillars of success

Every successful small business stands on three pillars at once: Pillar Standard to aim for Marketing (sales, promotion, public relations) Hit the mark every time Product or service Be the best available to your customer Integrity and credibility Beyond question

A simple route to opportunity

find an underserved market, learn exactly what it needs, then meet that need with your product or service.

Proactive versus reactive decisions

Proactive decisions build on strengths, chase untapped opportunities, test new offerings, track industry trends and remove threats early. Reactive decisions respond to weaknesses, quality failures, unhappy customers, low staff morale, competitor moves or a crisis. Every business makes both. The aim is to spend most of your time on the first list.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • What problem does my business solve, and for whom? What makes my business different from competitors, not just better? Which life cycle stage am I in, and what should my priorities be right now? Of the decisions I made last month, how many were proactive and how many were firefighting?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Step away from daily operations for a few hours each week to look at the business as a whole. You cannot see the forest while you are counting trees. Do not put problems "on the back burner". Postponing a decision is not a solution. Success is not a moment; it is a continuous process. Customers, staff, suppliers and competitors keep changing, and so must you.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Write a one-paragraph description of the problem you solve and your target customer List three ways your business is different from its nearest competitors Identify your current life cycle stage and your top three priorities for it Block a recurring weekly slot to review the business away from daily tasks

name: EJ 02 — Choosing a legal structure
description: Part: Foundations. Your legal structure decides who is liable for the business's debts, how profits are taxed, and how easily you can bring in investors. Choose it deliberately at the start, because changing later costs time and money.

Limited liability is not total protection

Banks often ask founders for personal guarantees, and directors can be personally liable for fraud, unpaid taxes or trading while insolvent.

lessons.name: Partnerships need a written agreement & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Partnerships need a written agreement; Investor readiness; Country focus; Individual                         None; Compliance obligations for an LLC

payload.html:
Partnerships need a written agreement

Set out each partner's contribution, profit share, decision rights, and what happens if a partner wants to leave, dies or falls out with the others.

Investor readiness

If you plan to raise equity from angel investors, impact funds or venture capital, a company with shares is usually expected. A clean share register and a shareholders' agreement make due diligence faster.

Country focus

Jordan In Jordan, most startups choose between an individual establishment and a limited liability company (LLC). finnpact generally recommends the LLC. Once a partner has paid their share of capital in full, they are not personally liable for the company's debts. Form Legal Owner liability Minimum Notes personality capital

Individual None

the Unlimited: all None Registered with the establishment business and personal Commercial Registry; owner are one assets at risk quick and cheap, but the owner carries every debt General or Separate Unlimited for None set Not recommended: limited general (joint) joint partners partnership partners become traders and are personally liable Limited liability Separate Limited to JOD 1 Most common; can company each partner's borrow, bid for share tenders, and convert to a shareholding company later; 50% of capital paid at registration, the rest within two years Private Separate Limited JOD Suits startups shareholding 50,000 planning structured company equity rounds with several investors

Compliance obligations for an LLC

Missing these can bring fines, suspension or an arbitrary tax assessment:

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Thresholds and fees change; Governance from day one

payload.html:
Overview

Keep the required commercial books (journal, correspondence book, inventory and balance sheet book) and retain them for ten years. Appoint a licensed auditor and file approved annual financial statements with the Companies Control Department. Submit an income tax self-assessment within four months of the year end. Register for general sales tax once revenue over 12 consecutive months reaches JOD 30,000 (services) or JOD 75,000 (trade and industry). File the beneficial owner form. Obtain a vocational licence from the municipality before trading. Enrol all employees in social security, whatever the headcount. With five or more employees, submit internal work regulations to the Ministry of Labour. Appoint a legal adviser if capital exceeds JOD 20,000.

Thresholds and fees change

Confirm current rules with the Companies Control Department or a lawyer before registering.

Governance from day one

Even a two-founder LLC benefits from basic governance: a clear manager or board, minutes of key decisions, partners' resolutions filed on time, and directors who do not compete with the company. Good governance is what investors and lenders check first.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • How much personal financial risk am I willing to carry? Will I need outside investors in the next two to three years? How will profits be taxed under each option, and how will I pay myself? If I have co-founders, have we agreed in writing who owns what and how decisions are made?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Keep business and personal money completely separate from day one, whatever structure you choose. Mixing funds is one of the most common and damaging mistakes founders make. Take advice from a local lawyer or accountant before registering. Tax treatment and filing duties vary widely between countries. Founder vesting (shares earned over time) protects the company if a co-founder leaves early.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Compare at least two structures available in your country on liability, tax and cost Confirm your choice with a qualified local adviser
  • Open a dedicated business bank account Sign a founders' or partnership agreement if you have co-owners

name: EJ 03 — Strategy, business planning and SWOT
description: Part: Strategy & Market. A business without direction drifts. Start with an honest SWOT analysis, turn it into a strategic plan with measurable objectives, and capture the essentials in a business plan you can show to lenders and investors.

lessons.name: Module 3 — Strategy, business planning and SWOT

payload.html: A business without direction drifts. Start with an honest SWOT analysis, turn it into a strategic plan with measurable objectives, and capture the essentials in a business plan you can show to lenders and investors.

lessons.name: SWOT analysis is a critical self-examination of your business & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: SWOT analysis is a critical self-examination of your business; Internal            Strengths; External            Opportunities; A SWOT is only useful if it leads to action; Some advisors now add a second T, for Trends; A strategic plan answers three questions; Execution matters more than the document

blocks.title: SWOT analysis is a critical self-examination of your business

payload.html:
SWOT analysis is a critical self-examination of your business

Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats come from outside. Helpful Harmful

Internal Strengths

specialist skills, good Weaknesses: skills gaps, poor equipment or premises, talented location, weak marketing, no clear people, intellectual property, strong direction, thin finances, high costs, relationships narrow product range, few customers or suppliers, weak brand

External Opportunities

new geographies, Threats: cheaper or better competing underserved markets, partnerships, technology, new rivals, imports, new acquiring a competitor, new products, taxes or regulations, rising interest hiring talent to open new markets rates and costs, tight credit, powerful customers squeezing prices

blocks.title: A SWOT is only useful if it leads to action

payload.html:
A SWOT is only useful if it leads to action

For each quadrant: 1. Strengths: use them more and build on them. 2. Weaknesses: fix or reduce them, starting with those that cost you customers. 3. Opportunities: decide which to pursue and what resources each needs. 4. Threats: plan how to reduce their impact before they arrive.

blocks.title: Some advisors now add a second T, for Trends

payload.html:
Some advisors now add a second T, for Trends

the shifts in technology, customer behaviour and regulation that will reshape your market.

blocks.title: A strategic plan answers three questions

payload.html:
A strategic plan answers three questions

where are we going, how will we get there, and what will it take? It sets short-term objectives (this year) and long-term objectives (three to five years), with precise financial targets and a view of your industry's outlook. There is no single right strategy. Options include focusing on a niche, competing on price, competing on quality or service, expanding geographically, or adding products. Strategic alliances let two or more businesses combine strengths to achieve more than either could alone. Before agreeing, settle how revenue or profit will be shared, who contributes what, who controls what, how risk is split, and who supplies which products or services. Vertical integration means moving up the supply chain (making your own inputs) or down it (selling direct to customers). It can cut costs and increase control but ties up capital. A business plan is a shorter, outward-facing version of your strategy, usually written at the formation stage. Typical contents: 1. Cover page and executive summary 2. Business profile: what you do, for whom, and why you are different 3. Market and competition 4. Marketing and sales plan 5. Operations and team 6. Financial information: projections, funding needed and how it will be used 7. Growth plan and milestones 8. Supporting documents

blocks.title: Execution matters more than the document

payload.html:
Execution matters more than the document

Assign each objective an owner and a deadline, review progress monthly, and update the plan when conditions change.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Validate demand before you spend; Size your market bottom-up; Example; Plan expansion in steps

payload.html:
Overview

Value proposition, validation and market size State your value proposition in one sentence. Use this formula: For [target customer] who [problem], we offer [solution]. Unlike [alternative], we [proof of difference]. Describe benefits, not features. "Online ordering site with a WhatsApp button" is a feature. "Never miss a lunchtime order again: customers order in 30 seconds" is a benefit.

Validate demand before you spend

You can run this four-step loop in about two weeks: 1. Listen: read competitors' reviews and comments in online groups for recurring complaints. 2. Ask: run ten short customer interviews or a quick poll. Ten good conversations beat a 200-person survey. 3. Measure: check search trends and keyword volumes, including seasonality, in the languages your customers use. 4. Test: launch a one-page offer or waitlist with a small, fixed ad budget, then count sign- ups, chats or pre-orders.

Size your market bottom-up

Multiply the number of realistic customers by the average revenue per customer per year. Investors trust this more than a top-down claim such as "we will win 1% of a USD 1 billion market". Use a top-down figure only as a sanity check.

Example

4,000 cafés and restaurants in your target cities × USD 600 a year in subscriptions = a USD 2.4 million addressable market. Show this for today and five years ahead, and state every assumption.

Plan expansion in steps

Start with one product for one customer segment, then sell a second product to the same segment, then take both to a new segment.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • What are my three biggest strengths and three most serious weaknesses? Which single opportunity would have the largest impact in the next 12 months? Which threat could put me out of business, and what is my plan for it? Are my objectives specific, measurable and dated?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Do your SWOT with someone outside the business, such as a mentor or a customer. Founders are often blind to their own weaknesses. Treat the SWOT and plan as living documents. Review them at least every quarter. If your current plan's objectives are not being met, ask why before writing new ones.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Complete a SWOT analysis with at least five points per quadrant Turn the SWOT into three to five strategic objectives with owners and dates Draft or update your business plan using the outline above Schedule a quarterly strategy review

name: EJ 04 — Marketing, customers and branding
description: Part: Strategy & Market. Marketing works when customers understand that your product delivers a benefit, fulfils a desire or solves a problem, and when that message reaches them consistently. Advertising is only one part of it; marketing covers everything that shapes how customers see and experience your business.

payload.html: Marketing works when customers understand that your product delivers a benefit, fulfils a desire or solves a problem, and when that message reaches them consistently. Advertising is only one part of it; marketing covers everything that shapes how customers see and experience your business.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; The basics of a marketing strategy; Market research before spending; Marketing goals; Branding is the emotional response people have to your business; Customer loyalty is cheaper than winning new customers; See what your customers see; Measure return on marketing spend; Choose two or three channels you can run every week; Make short video your core format

payload.html:
Overview

Marketing succeeds when it: tells customers clearly what benefit they get delivers its message consistently attracts new customers keeps existing customers buying changes buying behaviour in your favour

blocks.title: The basics of a marketing strategy

payload.html:
The basics of a marketing strategy

Know your core customers in detail. Keep product and service quality consistent. Keep every promise you make. Use several channels at once (online, social media, word of mouth, partnerships, events, direct sales) and adjust them as conditions change.

Market research before spending

Start cheaply: talk to 20 potential customers, study competitors' prices and reviews, and look at industry reports. Find out what customers want, how to improve what you already offer, and what would attract new buyers.

Marketing goals

Every campaign needs a defined scope (who it targets), a focus (one message), a priority (how it ranks against other work), and a measure of success.

blocks.title: Branding is the emotional response people have to your business

payload.html:
Branding is the emotional response people have to your business

its name, look, tone and, above all, the experience it delivers. A strong brand is earned through consistent delivery, not designed in a logo.

blocks.title: Customer loyalty is cheaper than winning new customers

payload.html:
Customer loyalty is cheaper than winning new customers

Tools include money-back guarantees, staff trained to serve well, fast and friendly service, loyalty rewards, and following up after each sale.

See what your customers see

Walk through your business as a customer: the website, the phone call, the premises, the invoice. Fix every point of friction.

Measure return on marketing spend

Set a marketing budget as a share of expected revenue, track which channel brought each customer, and move money towards what works. Digital marketing in practice In markets like Jordan and the wider region, almost every customer is online, mobile-first and reachable by video and WhatsApp. The question is not whether to be digital but which channels to run well.

blocks.title: Choose two or three channels you can run every week

payload.html:
Choose two or three channels you can run every week

Channel Best for Cost Instagram and Facebook Consumer brands, food, retail Low to medium and services, through Reels and Stories WhatsApp Business Closing sales, support and Free app; the business API repeat orders charges per template message Google Search and Maps Customers with high intent Free to medium (Business Profile) looking locally ("near me") LinkedIn B2B services, hiring and Medium to high investor visibility YouTube and Shorts Tutorials, demos and Low to medium storytelling Snapchat Under-35 consumers; under- Low to medium used by local competitors Email newsletter or Retention and an audience you Low; consent required WhatsApp Channel own

blocks.title: Make short video your core format

payload.html:
Make short video your core format

Keep it vertical and 15 to 45 seconds, with a hook in the first two seconds and subtitles. Film once and publish everywhere. Faces beat logos. Rotate four content pillars: educate (tips, myths), prove (testimonials, before and after), entertain (behind the scenes) and converse (polls, Q&A).

lessons.name: Be findable by search engines and AI assistants & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Be findable by search engines and AI assistants; Make it easy to pay; Use AI with guardrails; Follow the rules; Measure what matters; Aim for an LTV at least three times your CAC

blocks.title: Be findable by search engines and AI assistants

payload.html:
Be findable by search engines and AI assistants

Customers increasingly ask Google's AI answers or chat assistants for recommendations. Keep a fast mobile website with clear service and price pages, FAQs written the way customers ask, and a complete Google Business Profile. Use the same name, phone and address everywhere. Ask every satisfied customer for a review and reply to all of them. Never buy or fake reviews.

Make it easy to pay

Show instant payment options (for example CliQ in Jordan, or mobile wallets) in every ad, catalogue and invoice. A small incentive for paying upfront reduces failed deliveries and speeds up cash flow.

Use AI with guardrails

AI tools can draft posts, ads and visuals in minutes. Follow five rules: a person approves everything before it is published; a native speaker checks the Arabic; customer data never goes into public AI tools; no AI-generated testimonials or "customers"; and customers are told when they are chatting with a bot, with a human always available.

Follow the rules

Jordan's Personal Data Protection Law (No. 24 of 2023) requires explicit, recorded consent before you send marketing messages, plus an easy opt-out. Never buy or share contact lists. Advertising claims must be true under consumer protection law. Page owners can be liable for unlawful comments on their pages. In Gulf markets, influencers must be licensed, so ask for the licence before signing.

Measure what matters

Metric Formula Why it matters Click-through rate Clicks ÷ impressions Is the ad relevant? Cost per lead or sale Spend ÷ leads (or sales) The cost of one result Conversion rate Sales ÷ leads or chats Is your follow-up working? Customer acquisition All sales and marketing costs ÷ new The true cost of winning cost (CAC) customers a customer Return on ad spend Revenue from ads ÷ ad spend Do ads pay back? Customer lifetime value Average order × orders per year × What a customer is (LTV) years as a customer worth Response time Minutes to first reply Speed closes deals

blocks.title: Aim for an LTV at least three times your CAC

payload.html:
Aim for an LTV at least three times your CAC

Followers and likes are signals, not results.

lessons.name: A 90-day marketing plan
lessons.description: Covers: A 90-day marketing plan

payload.html:
A 90-day marketing plan

1. Days 1 to 30, foundations: write your persona and value proposition; set up your Business Profile, WhatsApp catalogue and payment details; start collecting contacts with consent; create a baseline metrics sheet. 2. Days 31 to 60, test: post three times a week, two of them videos; run one small click- to-WhatsApp campaign with three to five creatives; ask every customer for a review; review cost per lead and response time weekly. 3. Days 61 to 90, scale: double the budget on the best ad; run one creator or partner collaboration; launch a newsletter or WhatsApp Channel; check what AI search says about you.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Who exactly is my ideal customer, and where do they look for solutions like mine? Why do customers buy from me rather than a competitor? Have I asked them? Why have customers stopped buying from me? Which marketing channel brings the most profitable customers for each dollar spent? Can customers find and buy from me online?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Focus your marketing on the products or services with the highest gross margin (Module 7). Marketing is a work in progress. Test small, measure, and scale what works. Ask every new customer how they heard about you, and record it.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Write a one-page profile of your ideal customer Interview at least ten customers or prospects about their needs Set three marketing goals for the next quarter, each with a measure of success Set a monthly marketing budget and a way to track results by channel Walk through your business as a customer and list five improvements

name: EJ 05 — Operations, people and technology
description: Part: Strategy & Market. Well-run operations turn a good idea into a reliable business. This module covers leadership and urgency, effective and efficient processes, the supply chain, managing change, outsourcing, hiring, and the technology a startup needs.

payload.html: Well-run operations turn a good idea into a reliable business. This module covers leadership and urgency, effective and efficient processes, the supply chain, managing change, outsourcing, hiring, and the technology a startup needs.

lessons.name: Sense of urgency and leadership & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Sense of urgency and leadership; Time management; Effective versus efficient; Process improvement; Supply chain; Managing change; Outsourcing; People; Define the role and the skills needed before advertising; Country focus

payload.html:
Sense of urgency and leadership

Follow up, pay attention to detail, and deal with problems immediately rather than letting them grow. Good leaders inspire, encourage and challenge their teams.

Time management

Set goals, track progress, keep a prioritised to-do list, cut distractions, and delegate what others can do.

Effective versus efficient

An effective operation produces the result you intended. An efficient one produces it with the least wasted time, effort and money. You need both.

Process improvement

Change a process to standardise it, remove bottlenecks, reduce errors, simplify it, or fit a new system. Follow four steps: 1. Examine: find the areas performing below expectations. 2. Prioritise: rank them by their impact on customers, staff and profit. 3. Decide: choose what to change, starting with areas that repeatedly fail. 4. Document and implement: write down the new process, make sure everyone understands it, and check that it delivers the expected result.

Supply chain

Your supply chain is the flow of goods, information and money from your suppliers to your customers. Manage forecasting, purchasing, production, scheduling, stock levels, transport, payment terms and customer requests as one linked system.

Managing change

People resist change they do not understand. Lead from the front, state goals clearly, involve staff early, communicate openly, reward progress, and develop team leaders who can carry the change.

Outsourcing

Contract out functions you lack the skills for or need only part-time, such as bookkeeping, payroll, IT support, design or legal work. Compare the full cost of doing it in- house with the contractor's price and the quality you will get.

People

Hiring decisions shape your business more than almost anything else.

blocks.title: Define the role and the skills needed before advertising

payload.html:
Define the role and the skills needed before advertising

Use structured interviews and check references. Write a simple employee handbook covering conduct, leave, pay and safety. Get payroll and statutory deductions right every time, or outsource them. Give every new hire a proper orientation and initial training.

Country focus

Jordan employment and social security Jordan's Labour Law sets minimum standards that contracts can improve on but never reduce. Where a rule is unclear, courts read it in the worker's favour. Labour cases are heard quickly and free of court fees, so mistakes are costly for employers.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Employment contracts; Put contracts in writing, in Arabic, in two copies (one each); Ending employment; Social security (SSC)

payload.html:
Overview

Employee or contractor? The difference matters for social security and dismissal rights. Test Employee Contractor Control Works under your direction and Works independently, on their own supervision responsibility Paid for Being available during agreed hours Delivering the agreed result and place Business Carried by you Carried by the contractor risk
Employment contracts

blocks.title: Put contracts in writing, in Arabic, in two copies (one each)

payload.html:
Put contracts in writing, in Arabic, in two copies (one each)

Add a foreign-language copy for non-Arabic-speaking workers. A probation period must be written into the contract and may not exceed three months. It counts towards length of service. Normal working time is a maximum of 8 hours a day or 48 hours a week. Overtime is voluntary and paid at no less than 125% of normal pay. Work on the weekly rest day or a public holiday is paid at no less than 150%. Pay wages within seven days of the due date, at no less than the national minimum wage. Provide a safe workplace, legal leave (annual, sick and maternity) and safety equipment and training. Companies with five or more employees need written internal work regulations. Inventions belong to the employer if they relate to the business or use its information, tools or materials, unless agreed otherwise in writing. Put IP ownership in the contract.

Ending employment

Article 28 allows dismissal without notice only for serious misconduct. Examples include forged documents, serious damage caused by gross error, repeated safety breaches after two written warnings, unjustified absence (over 20 separate days a year or 10 consecutive days, after formal written warning), disclosing business secrets, assault, or being intoxicated at work. Unfair dismissal from an open- ended contract costs at least half a month's pay per year of service (minimum two months), plus notice pay and other entitlements. Ending a fixed-term contract early without cause means paying wages for the rest of the term.

Social security (SSC)

Enrolment is mandatory for every worker aged 16 or over, of any nationality, from the first employee. This includes self-employed people and owners or partners who work in the business. It covers work injury, old age, disability and death, maternity, unemployment and health insurance.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Budget for this in your hiring costs; Employer duties to SSC; Technology

payload.html:
Overview

Contribution (% of insurable wage, capped at JOD Employer Employee 3,000 a month) Old age, disability and death 11% 6.5% Work injury 2% – Maternity 0.75% – Unemployment 0.5% 1% Total (21.75%) 14.25% 7.5%

blocks.title: Budget for this in your hiring costs

payload.html:
Budget for this in your hiring costs

a JOD 600 monthly salary costs the business about JOD 685.50 once the employer's contribution is added.

Employer duties to SSC

pay contributions by the 15th of the following month (late interest is 1% a month); report new joiners and leavers by the end of the following month; and file the annual staff list by the end of March. Penalties include a 30% surcharge on under-declared wages, a JOD 500 fine for each uninsured worker, and JOD 1,000 to 2,000 for knowingly false data.

Technology

Choose software to fit your business needs, not the other way round. Back up all files to the cloud automatically. Protect devices and accounts with strong passwords, two-factor authentication and up-to-date security software. Use the internet and mobile tools to reach customers and work from anywhere.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Which process causes the most errors, delays or customer complaints? Which tasks take my time that someone else could do better or cheaper?
  • If my laptop were stolen today, what would I lose? Does every employee know what is expected of them and how they are doing?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Measure before and after every process change so you know whether it worked. Fix one bottleneck at a time; the next one will become visible once the first is gone. Founders often hire too fast when busy and fire too slowly when a hire is not working. Do the opposite.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Map your core process from order to delivery and mark the bottlenecks Choose one process to improve using the four steps above List functions you could outsource and compare the costs Set up automatic cloud backup and two-factor authentication on key accounts Draft a basic employee handbook and onboarding checklist

name: EJ 06 — Reading your financial statements
description: Part: Financial Health. Three statements tell you how your business is really doing: the income statement (profit), the balance sheet (what you own and owe), and the cash flow statement (where cash came from and went). A founder who can read them makes better decisions and earns the trust of lenders and investors.

payload.html: Three statements tell you how your business is really doing: the income statement (profit), the balance sheet (what you own and owe), and the cash flow statement (where cash came from and went). A founder who can read them makes better decisions and earns the trust of lenders and investors.

lessons.name: The three statements at a glance & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: The three statements at a glance; Profit is not cash; Look at trends, not single years; Common-size statements; Cash versus accrual accounting

blocks.title: The three statements at a glance

payload.html:
The three statements at a glance

Statement Question it answers Covers Income statement Did we make a profit? Revenue, cost of sales, expenses (profit and loss) and net profit over a period Balance sheet What do we own and owe? Assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a point in time Statement Question it answers Covers Cash flow statement Where did our cash come Cash from operating, investing from and go? and financing activities over a period

Profit is not cash

A profitable business can still run out of money if customers pay late, stock piles up or loan repayments fall due. The cash flow statement shows cash actually received and paid. It leaves out non-cash items such as depreciation.

blocks.title: Look at trends, not single years

payload.html:
Look at trends, not single years

Put three to five years (or 12 to 24 months for a young startup) side by side, oldest on the left and newest on the right. Add your projections to the right. Adjust for "abnormal" items. To see the true profit of the business, strip out or correct items that distort it: personal expenses run through the business, deals with relatives not at market price, owner salaries far above or below market, one-off gains or losses, and corrections of past errors.

Common-size statements

Convert each line into a percentage of revenue (income statement) or of total assets (balance sheet). Percentages make it easy to spot unusual changes, as in this example: Line Year 1 (USD) % of revenue Year 2 (USD) % of revenue Revenue 200,000 100% 260,000 100% Cost of sales 120,000 60% 169,000 65% Gross profit 80,000 40% 91,000 35% Operating expenses 60,000 30% 70,200 27% Net profit 20,000 10% 20,800 8% Revenue grew 30%, but gross margin fell from 40% to 35%. The founder should find out why: rising supplier prices, discounting, or a shift towards lower-margin products.

Cash versus accrual accounting

Cash accounting records income when paid and costs when settled. Accrual accounting records them when earned or incurred. Accrual gives a truer picture of performance and is usually required once a business grows or raises finance.

lessons.name: Five financial pitfalls to avoid & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Five financial pitfalls to avoid; Country focus; Income tax; How taxable income is calculated; Less, in order; Records and returns; Tax accounting is on an accruals basis; Withholding tax you must deduct and pay over; Penalties

payload.html:
Five financial pitfalls to avoid

1. No cash reserve for slow months or emergencies 2. Not tracking cash flow weekly 3. Borrowing without a clear plan to repay 4. Spending ahead of revenue 5. Mixing personal and business money

Country focus

Jordan income tax and sales tax Tax shapes your prices, cash flow and record-keeping from the first sale. Here are the basics every Jordanian founder should know.

Income tax

what is taxed. Any income earned in or from Jordan is taxable, for residents and non-residents alike, unless the law specifically exempts it. Exemptions include end- of-service payments within legal limits and some agricultural income: the first JOD 1 million of an individual's agricultural sales, or the first JOD 50,000 of a company's net agricultural income.

How taxable income is calculated

Step Example (JOD) Gross income from taxable sources 250 Less allowable expenses (50) Net income 200

Less, in order

losses carried forward, personal and – family exemptions (individuals), approved donations Taxable income 200 Tax is charged on taxable income at the rates set for individuals or companies. Companies also pay a national contribution on taxable income: 1% for most companies (2% for telecoms and insurance, 3% for banks, 7% for basic mining). Individuals pay 1% on taxable income above JOD 200,000.
Records and returns

blocks.title: Tax accounting is on an accruals basis

payload.html:
Tax accounting is on an accruals basis

Only some professionals (lawyers, doctors, auditors) may use cash accounting. Records must follow international accounting standards and be audited by a licensed auditor. Tax law requires records to be kept for at least four years after filing, and longer while any dispute is open. Commercial law requires the statutory books to be kept for ten years, so keep everything for ten. File the annual return within four months of the year end.

blocks.title: Withholding tax you must deduct and pay over

payload.html:
Withholding tax you must deduct and pay over

Payment Rate Who withholds Professional fees paid by a 5% The paying company company Employee salaries Per the tax Employer regulations Bank interest to an individual 5% The bank Bank interest to a company 7% The bank Imported services paid to a non- 10% The resident business receiving resident the service

Penalties

Late filing costs JOD 100 for individuals, JOD 300 for most companies and JOD 1,000 for shareholding companies. Failing to keep records, withhold tax, produce documents or issue an invoice on request costs JOD 200 to 500 each. Late payment adds 0.4% a week. Tax evasion, such as fake documents, hidden income or destroyed records, brings a fine equal to the tax evaded, and imprisonment for repeat offences.

lessons.name: General sales tax (a VAT-style tax)
lessons.description: Covers: General sales tax (a VAT-style tax)

payload.html:
General sales tax (a VAT-style tax)

Tax is charged at each stage of the supply chain. Registered businesses deduct the tax paid on their inputs from the tax they collect on sales. Registration is compulsory once sales over 12 consecutive months reach JOD 30,000 for services or JOD 75,000 for trade and industry. Voluntary registration is possible. Zero-rated versus exempt. Both charge customers no tax. But input tax can be reclaimed on zero-rated sales, including exports, and cannot be reclaimed on exempt sales. Tax invoices and periodic returns are required from the date of registration. Penalties. Registering up to 60 days late costs JOD 100 to 500. Beyond 60 days, the fine is two to three times the tax due plus a JOD 200 to 1,000 fine. Under-declaring sales or over-claiming input tax beyond set limits is treated as a crime. Late payment adds 0.4% a week. Build sales tax into your prices (Module 7) and your cash budget (Module 10). Tax collected from customers is not your money. Set it aside until it is paid over. Rates and thresholds change, so confirm current figures with the Income and Sales Tax Department or a tax adviser.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Do I receive monthly financial statements, and do I read them? Is my profit rising faster or slower than my revenue? Why? Which personal or one-off items are distorting my figures? How many months could I survive on the cash I hold today?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Hire a competent bookkeeper or use cloud accounting software from the start. Clean books cost far less than cleaning them up later. Read the cash flow statement first. It is the hardest to manipulate and the one that kills startups. Ask your accountant to explain any line you do not understand.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Obtain your latest income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement Build a side-by-side spreadsheet covering every period you have Prepare a common-size version and flag any line that moved by more than 3 percentage points List any abnormal or personal items and adjust for them Set a target cash reserve (for example, three months of fixed costs)

name: EJ 07 — Revenue, gross margin and expense control
description: Part: Financial Health. Total revenue tells you how big you are; gross margin by product tells you where you actually make money. Analyse both, then review every expense line for savings.

lessons.name: Module 7 — Revenue, gross margin and expense control

payload.html: Total revenue tells you how big you are; gross margin by product tells you where you actually make money. Analyse both, then review every expense line for savings.

lessons.name: Gross profit and gross margin & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Gross profit and gross margin; Analyse by product or service line; Pricing; Sales terms; Growing revenue; Reviewing expenses; Professional fees (accounting, legal)

payload.html:
Gross profit and gross margin

Gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of what you sold. Gross margin is gross profit as a percentage of revenue. It is the money left to pay overheads and generate profit.

blocks.title: Analyse by product or service line

payload.html:
Analyse by product or service line

A business can be profitable overall while some products lose money. In this example the business earns a 34% overall margin, but Product C earns only 20%: Product line Revenue (USD) Direct costs (USD) Gross profit (USD) Gross margin Product B 60,000 30,000 30,000 50% Product A 100,000 70,000 30,000 30% Product C 40,000 32,000 8,000 20% Total 200,000 132,000 68,000 34% Product B earns as much gross profit as Product A on 40% less revenue. Marketing effort should lean towards B; Product C needs a price rise, a cheaper supplier, or a decision to drop it.

Pricing

Know how each price was set: cost plus a mark-up, competitor matching, or the value to the customer. Test price changes and watch the effect on both revenue and gross profit.

Sales terms

Payment terms, deposits, credit limits and instalment options can win or lose sales and strongly affect cash flow.

Growing revenue

Look for underserved market segments, new channels (especially online), complementary products or services, and new revenue streams. Check that you have the capacity and capital to handle growth.

Reviewing expenses

Go through each overhead line and ask whether it is necessary, whether it delivers value, and whether it could be cheaper. Common savings areas:

Professional fees (accounting, legal)

get competing quotes; use standard templates for routine documents Advertising: compare spend with the sales it generates Subscriptions and memberships: cancel those you do not use Equipment: compare leasing with buying Insurance: confirm cover is adequate and re-quote every year Interest: know every rate you pay and pay off the most expensive debt first Rent: negotiate terms before renewal Telephone and internet: bundle services and review plans Miscellaneous: reclassify anything over a small threshold so you can see what it is

lessons.name: Expense claims & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Expense claims; Variance notes; Know your costs; Direct (variable) costs rise and fall with what you produce; Break-even point

payload.html:
Expense claims

Require receipts, a business purpose and approval by someone other than the claimant. Never rubber-stamp claims.

Variance notes

Each month, write one line explaining any revenue or expense item that changed significantly from the previous period or from budget. This builds a record that makes later decisions faster. Costing and pricing a new product or service Pricing is a strategic decision, not just a number. It decides whether you make a profit, how the market sees you (premium, mid-range or budget) and how well you can compete. Before setting a price, answer five questions: What does it really cost me? What value does the customer get? What do competitors charge? How price-sensitive are my customers? What is my pricing goal: profit, market entry, new customers or expansion?

Know your costs

Split them into two groups:

blocks.title: Direct (variable) costs rise and fall with what you produce

payload.html:
Direct (variable) costs rise and fall with what you produce

raw materials, direct labour hours, packaging, delivery, sales commissions, and energy used in production. Fixed (indirect) costs stay the same whatever you produce: management and admin salaries, rent, audit and legal fees, insurance, bank interest, internet and utilities. Unit cost is the total cost of producing and selling one unit in a period. It falls as volume rises, because fixed costs are spread over more units. With fixed costs of JOD 1,000 a month: Month Units made Direct costs (JOD) Fixed costs (JOD) Unit cost (JOD) June 100 1,000 1,000 20 Month Units made Direct costs (JOD) Fixed costs (JOD) Unit cost (JOD) September 50 500 1,000 30 August 5 50 1,000 210 You can cut unit cost by finding cheaper inputs, outsourcing production, growing volume, or reducing overheads.

Break-even point

This is where total revenue equals total costs. Divide fixed costs by the profit each unit contributes (selling price minus variable cost per unit). Example: fixed costs of JOD 1,000 a month, variable cost of JOD 3 a unit and a price of JOD 5 give a contribution of JOD 2. You must sell 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 units a month to break even.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Accounting profit versus economic profit; Common pricing strategies; Worked example

payload.html:
Overview

Price taker or price maker? A price taker sells something with close substitutes, such as dairy, soft drinks or vegetables, and must accept the market price. A price maker has a differentiated product with no close substitute and can set the price. Know which you are before choosing a strategy.

Accounting profit versus economic profit

Accounting profit is revenue minus costs. Economic profit also deducts the opportunity cost: what your time and money would earn elsewhere. A founder who leaves a well-paid job should check that the business beats the salary given up, not just that it shows a profit.

Common pricing strategies

Strategy How it works Example Cost-plus Add a set margin to unit cost Unit cost JOD 10 plus a 40% mark-up = price JOD 14 Value-based Price on the value customers Innovative products that solve a perceive, not just cost real problem, premium brands Market-based Set the price within competitors' Competitors charge JOD 15 to 18; range you charge JOD 16 Penetration Start low, or with a free trial, to Gyms, internet services win share, then raise gradually Skimming Start high for early adopters, New phones and TVs, fashion then lower as the market items matures Strategy How it works Example Freemium or A free basic version and a paid Many technology startups subscription version with extra features Pricing too low means losing money without noticing, signalling low quality, and struggling to raise prices later. Pricing too high means losing customers to competitors unless the value clearly justifies it.

Worked example

a ticket-booking app. Development costs 100 hours at JOD 10 an hour (JOD 1,000), plus JOD 300 of software subscriptions and JOD 700 of hosting: JOD 2,000 in direct costs. Fixed costs are JOD 4,000, so the total cost is JOD 6,000. A 50% target margin sets a revenue target of JOD 9,000.

lessons.name: Monthly subscription of JOD 5 (JOD 60 a year) & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Monthly subscription of JOD 5 (JOD 60 a year); Remember that sales tax is added to the price; After launch; Pricing mistakes to avoid

blocks.title: Monthly subscription of JOD 5 (JOD 60 a year)

payload.html:
Monthly subscription of JOD 5 (JOD 60 a year)

150 subscribers needed. One-off lifetime fee of JOD 5: 1,800 subscribers needed. One-off lifetime fee of JOD 100: 90 subscribers needed.

blocks.title: Remember that sales tax is added to the price

payload.html:
Remember that sales tax is added to the price

Decide whether the customer, the business or both will bear it.

After launch

test and adjust. Run split tests that change one variable at a time (price point, features, segment or payment timing). Gather customer feedback and watch sales data for the effect on volume and profit. Your price is right when sales are healthy, you make a profit, customers are satisfied, competitors cannot easily take your customers, and the price reflects value, not just cost.

Pricing mistakes to avoid

setting prices on gut feeling instead of numbers; copying a competitor exactly; pricing low only to attract customers; ignoring indirect costs; changing prices constantly without reason. Also allow for the economy and customers' purchasing power, regulated price limits, distributors' margins, and enough flexibility to respond to competitors and demand.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Which of my products or services has the highest gross margin? Am I selling enough of it? How did I set my prices, and when did I last review them? What do competitors offer that I do not? What would happen to profit if I raised prices by 5%?
  • Which expense has grown fastest, and why?

Practical advice from experience:

  • A small price increase usually adds more to profit than a much larger rise in volume. Recheck supplier prices at least once a year. Review your largest five expense lines every month; they hold most of the savings.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Calculate gross margin for each product or service line Rank lines by gross profit, not revenue, and adjust marketing focus Review the pricing of your lowest-margin line Go through every expense line and identify at least three savings Introduce a written expense-claim policy Start a monthly one-page variance note

name: EJ 08 — Assets, liabilities and working capital
description: Part: Financial Health. Founders watch revenue and costs closely but often neglect the balance sheet. Yet slow- paying customers, excess stock and unmanaged debts are what drain a startup's cash.

lessons.name: Module 8 — Assets, liabilities and working capital

payload.html: Founders watch revenue and costs closely but often neglect the balance sheet. Yet slow- paying customers, excess stock and unmanaged debts are what drain a startup's cash.

lessons.name: Book value is not market value & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Book value is not market value; Assets to review; Liabilities to review; Hidden and contingent liabilities

blocks.title: Book value is not market value

payload.html:
Book value is not market value

Book value is what you paid for an asset minus accumulated depreciation. Fair market value is what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, both well informed and under no pressure. Lenders and buyers care about market value.

Assets to review

Asset What to check Accounts receivable (money owed by Is there an aged list (current, 30, 60, 90+ customers) days)? How do you assess a customer before giving credit? Are your terms enforced? Asset What to check Inventory (stock) Do you hold the right items in the right quantities? Do you mark down slow-moving stock quickly? Equipment and property Is each item fully used? Owned or leased? Is money set aside for repairs and replacement? Cash and petty cash Is petty cash locked, receipted and reviewed monthly? Prepayments and staff advances Can prepayments be reduced to free cash? Are advances recorded and recovered? Vehicles Owned or leased? How is business use of personal vehicles reimbursed?

Liabilities to review

Liability What to check Accounts payable (money owed to Are all bills recorded? Any overdue, attracting suppliers) late fees or holding up orders? Are early- payment discounts taken? Overdrafts and credit cards Are overdrafts routine? What interest rate applies to each card? Long-term loans Can repayments be met from operating profit? Could the debt be restructured on better terms? Customer deposits Could you refund them if needed? Taxes and employee benefits Are they paid on time? Are amounts owed set aside?

Hidden and contingent liabilities

Some obligations do not appear on the balance sheet: long-term leases, pending legal claims, warranty work, prepaid vouchers, and unfunded staff benefits. List them and consider setting cash aside.

lessons.name: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities; Worked example; Levers to shrink the gap

blocks.title: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities

payload.html:
Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities

It is the cushion that funds day- to-day operations. Too little and you cannot pay bills; too much idle cash means a missed opportunity to invest in growth. Your working capital requirement Every trading business buys from suppliers, holds stock and sells to customers. The money tied up in that cycle is your working capital requirement, also called the funding gap. It is the heart of the business, and the main reason fast-growing startups run out of cash. \text{Working capital requirement} = \text{Inventory} + \text{Receivables} - \text{Payables} Each part can be estimated from revenue and the number of days involved: Receivables = days of credit given × (annual revenue ÷ 365) Inventory = days of stock held × (annual cost of sales ÷ 365) Payables = days of credit received × (annual cost of sales ÷ 365)

Worked example

Annual revenue is USD 182,500 (USD 500 a day) and gross margin is 40%, so cost of sales is USD 300 a day. Component Well-managed Amount % of Slipping Amount % of terms (USD) revenue terms (USD) revenue Receivables 45 days 22,500 12.3% 90 days 45,000 24.7% Inventory 30 days 9,000 4.9% 120 days 36,000 19.7% Less 20 days −6,000 −3.3% 20 days −6,000 −3.3% payables Requirement 25,500 13.9% 75,000 41.1% With well-managed terms, a new USD 40,000 contract needs about USD 5,560 of extra working capital (13.9%). If collections and stock control slip, the same contract needs USD 16,440 (41.1%), nearly three times as much. That is cash you must find from an overdraft, a loan or your own pocket.

Levers to shrink the gap

collect faster, hold less stock, and negotiate longer terms with suppliers. Agree longer terms upfront rather than simply paying late; overdue accounts soon lead to supply problems. Factoring means selling your receivables to a third party at a discount for immediate cash. It helps cash flow but is expensive; use it with care.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • How many days, on average, do my customers take to pay? How much cash is tied up in slow-moving stock? Am I paying any supplier late? What is it costing me? What obligations could hit me that are not on my balance sheet?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Invoice immediately and follow up on the first day an invoice is overdue. Agree payment terms with suppliers that are at least as long as the terms you give customers. Ask for deposits on large or custom orders.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Produce an aged receivables list and chase everything over 30 days Identify stock that has not moved in 90 days and plan to clear it List every debt with its balance, interest rate and repayment date List contingent liabilities and estimate their possible cost Calculate your working capital

name: EJ 09 — Key financial ratios, your business dashboard
description: Part: Financial Health. A handful of ratios, tracked every month or quarter, warn you of trouble long before it shows in the bank balance. No ratio is good or bad on its own; what matters is its trend and how it compares with businesses like yours.

lessons.name: Module 9 — Key financial ratios, your business dashboard

payload.html: A handful of ratios, tracked every month or quarter, warn you of trouble long before it shows in the bank balance. No ratio is good or bad on its own; what matters is its trend and how it compares with businesses like yours.

lessons.name: Eleven core ratios & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Eleven core ratios; Worked example

payload.html:
Eleven core ratios

Ratio Formula What it tells you Current ratio Current assets ÷ current Can you pay bills due within a liabilities year? Below 1 is a warning sign. Quick (acid-test) ratio (Cash + receivables) ÷ The same test, excluding stock, current liabilities which may be slow to sell Working capital Current assets − current The cash cushion available to liabilities run and grow the business Receivables turnover Credit sales ÷ average How many times a year you receivables collect what customers owe Days to collect (Receivables ÷ credit sales) × Average days customers take 365 to pay Inventory turnover Cost of sales ÷ average How many times a year you sell inventory through your stock Days in inventory (Ending inventory ÷ cost of How many days of sales are sales) × 365 sitting in stock Debt to equity Total liabilities ÷ owner's How much of the business is equity funded by creditors versus owners Interest cover (times Profit before interest and tax How comfortably profit covers interest earned) ÷ interest expense interest payments Net profit margin Net profit ÷ net sales How much of each sale becomes profit Asset turnover Net sales ÷ average total How well your assets generate assets sales

Worked example

A startup has USD 50,000 in current assets (of which USD 15,000 is stock) and USD 25,000 in current liabilities.

lessons.name: Current ratio & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Current ratio; Choose the ratios that matter for your business

payload.html:
Current ratio

50,000 ÷ 25,000 = 2.0 Quick ratio: (50,000 − 15,000) ÷ 25,000 = 1.4 Working capital: 50,000 − 25,000 = USD 25,000 If credit sales for the year are USD 180,000 and receivables are USD 30,000, days to collect = (30,000 ÷ 180,000) × 365 = about 61 days. If your terms are 30 days, customers are paying twice as slowly as agreed.

blocks.title: Choose the ratios that matter for your business

payload.html:
Choose the ratios that matter for your business

A service business with no stock can ignore the inventory ratios. A retailer should watch them closely.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Which five ratios best describe the health of my business? Are they improving or getting worse over the last four quarters? How do they compare with others in my industry?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Set up a simple spreadsheet that calculates your chosen ratios automatically from your monthly accounts. Lenders and investors will calculate these ratios anyway. Know your numbers before they ask. Ask your industry association or bank for typical ratios in your sector.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Choose five to seven ratios relevant to your business Calculate them for each period you have data for Plot the trend and flag any ratio moving the wrong way Agree one action for each ratio that is getting worse

name: EJ 10 — Budgets, forecasts and cash flow
description: Part: Planning & Funding. A budget is where you intend to go; a forecast is where you are actually heading. Compare the two every month, explain the gaps, and keep a rolling cash budget so you are never surprised by a shortfall.

lessons.name: Module 10 — Budgets, forecasts and cash flow

payload.html: A budget is where you intend to go; a forecast is where you are actually heading. Compare the two every month, explain the gaps, and keep a rolling cash budget so you are never surprised by a shortfall.

lessons.name: Budget versus forecast & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Budget versus forecast; The budgets a startup needs; Types of budget; Budget variance report; Cash budget example; The equipment purchase in month 1 reduces cash by a quarter

payload.html:
Budget versus forecast

A budget is a financial target you commit to hitting. A forecast is your best estimate of results based on current performance and the economic climate. A stretch budget sets deliberately ambitious targets to push the team.

The budgets a startup needs

1. Sales budget: expected revenue by product and month. 2. Expense budget: expected operating costs by month. 3. Capital expenditure budget: planned purchases of equipment and other long-term assets, and their effect on future profit. 4. Cash budget: expected cash in and out each month. This is the most important for a startup.

Types of budget

Type How it works When to use it Static Set once for the year and not changed Stable, predictable businesses Rolling Each time a month or quarter ends, a new Startups and fast-changing one is added, so you always look 12 months businesses ahead Fixed Amounts stay the same regardless of Fixed costs such as rent activity Flexible Amounts adjust with sales volume; can Variable costs and scenario include best and worst cases planning

Budget variance report

Each month compare actual results with budget, mark each variance favourable or unfavourable, and explain the significant ones. Line Budget Actual Variance Favourable or unfavourable (USD) (USD) (USD) Revenue 50,000 46,000 −4,000 Unfavourable Cost of 30,000 27,000 3,000 Favourable (lower sales sales volume) Marketing 3,000 4,500 −1,500 Unfavourable Rent 3,000 3,000 0 On budget

Cash budget example

A three-month cash budget shows the timing of cash, not profit: Line (USD) Month 1 Month 2 Month 3 Opening cash 20,000 15,000 19,000 Cash sales 15,000 16,000 18,000 Collections from customers 10,000 14,000 15,000 Total cash in 25,000 30,000 33,000 Supplier payments 12,000 13,000 14,000 Salaries 8,000 8,000 9,000 Rent 3,000 3,000 3,000 Other operating costs 2,000 2,000 2,000 Equipment purchase 5,000 0 0 Loan repayment 0 0 4,000 Total cash out 30,000 26,000 32,000 Net cash flow −5,000 4,000 1,000 Closing cash 15,000 19,000 20,000

blocks.title: The equipment purchase in month 1 reduces cash by a quarter

payload.html:
The equipment purchase in month 1 reduces cash by a quarter

If the minimum safe balance is USD 15,000, there is no room for a slow month. The founder could lease the equipment or negotiate longer supplier terms.

lessons.name: Managing cash flow day to day The three Cs of cash flow & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Managing cash flow day to day The three Cs of cash flow; Speed up money coming in; Invoice immediately and follow up the day a payment is late; Slow down money going out, sensibly; Use the full payment terms you are given; If cash gets tight, pay in this order; Know your break-even point; Build a simple financial model

blocks.title: Managing cash flow day to day The three Cs of cash flow

payload.html:
Managing cash flow day to day The three Cs of cash flow

1. Cash: tight control of headcount and every expense, and finding cash where you least expect it, such as faster collections, unused assets or grants for product development. 2. Credit: a working plan for payments in and payments out, including agreed deferrals with creditors. Good supplier relationships make this far easier. 3. Communication: do not hide difficulties. Talk early to your bank, suppliers, key customers and staff about the steps you are taking. People support a business that is open with them.
Speed up money coming in

blocks.title: Invoice immediately and follow up the day a payment is late

payload.html:
Invoice immediately and follow up the day a payment is late

Ask for deposits when orders are taken. Credit-check every new customer you sell to on credit. Offer a small discount for prompt payment. Clear old and obsolete stock for whatever it will fetch.

blocks.title: Slow down money going out, sensibly

payload.html: Slow down money going out, sensibly

blocks.title: Use the full payment terms you are given

payload.html:
Use the full payment terms you are given

if a bill is due in 30 days, do not pay in 15. Weigh early-payment discounts carefully. Some are good value; others amount to an expensive loan to your supplier. Do not always choose the cheapest supplier; better payment terms can help cash flow more. Finance long-term assets with long-term loans or leases, not working capital.

blocks.title: If cash gets tight, pay in this order

payload.html:
If cash gets tight, pay in this order

salaries first (unpaid staff soon leave), then critical suppliers, then agree partial or deferred payments with everyone else.

Know your break-even point

Calculate the monthly sales you need to cover all costs. It gives you a clear first target and anchors your cash projections.

Build a simple financial model

A model combines your actual results with assumptions about the future, so you can ask "what if?": prices rise 5%, a key customer leaves, we hire two people. Start with expenses, because spending drives revenue and is within your control. Then link revenue to the activities that generate it, such as marketing spend, sales staff and conversion rates. Update the model monthly with actual figures. Fewer than half of startups keep a working model, and those that do make faster, better decisions.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Do I have a written budget for this year? Do I compare it with actual results? What is my lowest projected cash balance in the next six months, and when does it occur? What would happen if sales came in 20% below budget?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Update your cash budget weekly in the early months.
  • Build a worst-case scenario and know what you would cut first. Arrange finance before you need it. Banks lend more readily to businesses that are not desperate.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Prepare a 12-month sales and expense budget Build a rolling 13-week or 12-month cash budget Set a minimum cash balance and a trigger for action Produce a variance report every month and explain significant gaps List planned equipment purchases in a capital expenditure budget

name: EJ 11 — Financing your startup
description: Part: Planning & Funding. Every source of money has a price: debt must be repaid with interest, and equity costs you a share of ownership. Match the type of finance to what you need it for, and raise it before you are desperate.

payload.html: Every source of money has a price: debt must be repaid with interest, and equity costs you a share of ownership. Match the type of finance to what you need it for, and raise it before you are desperate.

lessons.name: Debt versus equity & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Debt versus equity; Sources of finance; What funders look for

payload.html:
Debt versus equity

Debt financing Equity financing What it is Borrowed money Money invested in exchange for a share of the business Repayment Must be repaid with interest, on a No repayment; investors share in schedule profits and in the value when sold Control You keep ownership; lenders may You give up part of the ownership impose conditions and often some control Cost Interest (often tax-deductible) Share of future value; investors expect a high return Best for Assets, stock and working capital in a High-growth ventures that cannot business with steady cash flow yet support repayments How much ownership you give up depends on how much the investor puts in, how long you have traded, your track record, and your future prospects. Ask yourself: is it better to own all of something small or part of something much larger?

Sources of finance

Source Type Notes Personal savings Equity Shows commitment to other funders Friends and family Debt or equity Put terms in writing to protect relationships Grants and development Usually non-repayable or Government, donor and impact programmes concessional programmes; often tied to milestones and reporting Bank overdraft or credit Debt Flexible working capital; usually line renewed annually Bank term or instalment Debt For equipment, premises or loan expansion; usually needs collateral or a guarantee Receivables finance and Debt Cash against unpaid invoices; factoring costly but fast Supplier (vendor) credit Debt Longer payment terms from suppliers; often the cheapest finance available Leasing Debt-like Use equipment without buying it; the lessor keeps ownership Credit cards Debt Convenient but very expensive; short-term only Borrowing against your Debt Puts your home at risk; use only home with great care Angel investors Equity Individuals investing early, often bringing advice and contacts Venture capital and Equity For scalable businesses; expect impact funds strong growth and an exit plan Source Type Notes Merger or public listing Equity Later-stage options for established businesses

What funders look for

A clear business plan, accurate financial statements, a realistic cash budget showing how the money will be used and repaid, evidence of demand, and a capable team.

lessons.name: Overview & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Overview; Pre-money valuation; Example; Higher is not always better; Pitching to funders

payload.html:
Overview

Funding by stage The right source of money depends on how far the business has come: Stage What you are doing Typical sources Idea and early Developing the idea, building a Own savings (bootstrapping), product first version friends and family, grants Launch and First customers, proving Accelerators and incubators, validation demand grants, angels, crowdfunding Seed Building the team and a Angel groups, seed funds, impact repeatable sales model investors, bank or programme loans Growth (Series A Scaling and moving towards Venture capital, growth and and beyond) profitability impact funds, larger bank facilities Equity is cheap at the start but becomes the most expensive money as the company's value rises. Debt has a fixed, known cost and you keep your ownership. Valuation basics A startup's valuation is agreed between founders and investors when a round is raised. In practice it depends as much on investor demand as on revenue, the team, the market and competition.

Pre-money valuation

value before the new investment. Post-money valuation: pre-money value plus the new investment. Investor stake: investment ÷ post-money valuation.

Example

at a USD 2 million pre-money valuation, an investor putting in USD 500,000 gets a post-money value of USD 2.5 million and a 20% stake.

Higher is not always better

An inflated valuation is hard to grow into, risks a "down round" later, and makes staff share options less attractive. Price friends-and-family rounds fairly too. A valuation that later investors will not accept may force an awkward restructuring.

Pitching to funders

the finnpact pitch deck Structure your pitch around the questions funders ask: 1. Problem: what unmet need or gap are you addressing? 2. Solution: how does your product or service solve it? 3. Value proposition: what makes you unique, and why would customers choose you? 4. Competitive analysis: who else serves this market, and how do you compare? 5. Business model: how do you make money? One-off or recurring, B2B or B2C, pricing assumptions? 6. Market traction: sales, customers, publicity and well-known clients so far. 7. Go-to-market: which segments you will target and how you will reach them. 8. Revenue growth and financials: actual results plus at least two years of projections, with key assumptions. 9. The ask: how much you need and exactly how it will be used (equipment, stock, staff, marketing, IT). 10. People: key team members and planned hiring, including the gender split of staff. 11. Impact: the Sustainable Development Goals you contribute to and how you improve people's lives.

Practical advice from experience:

  • Do not use short-term debt such as overdrafts or credit cards to fund long-term assets. Prepare a funding pack (business plan, last statements, cash budget, use of funds) before approaching anyone. Read every term sheet and loan agreement with a lawyer or advisor.

Before moving on, complete:
