name: EJ 12 — Internal controls, risk and fraud prevention
description: Part: Protection. Small businesses suffer fraud too, often at the hands of trusted staff, and a single large loss can sink a startup. Simple controls, set up early, make errors and theft far less likely and your financial data far more reliable.

lessons.name: Module 12 — Internal controls, risk and fraud prevention

payload.html: Small businesses suffer fraud too, often at the hands of trusted staff, and a single large loss can sink a startup. Simple controls, set up early, make errors and theft far less likely and your financial data far more reliable.

lessons.name: Why controls matter & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Why controls matter; The fraud triangle; Common forms of fraud; Key controls by area; Segregation of duties

payload.html:
Why controls matter

Good controls make staff follow company policy, reduce errors, produce reliable financial information, improve efficiency, and protect assets. No set of controls is foolproof, so check them with occasional surprise reviews.

The fraud triangle

Fraud usually needs three things at once: 1. Opportunity: weak controls, one person handling a whole transaction, no reviews. 2. Pressure or motive: personal debt, financial stress, unrealistic targets. 3. Rationalisation: "I'm underpaid", "I'll pay it back", "no one will notice". You cannot control pressure or rationalisation, but you can remove the opportunity. Remove the opportunity and most fraud never happens.

Common forms of fraud

theft of cash or assets, false or hidden information, bribery, extortion, undisclosed conflicts of interest, forgery, theft of trade secrets, and breaches of trust by people managing money on your behalf.

Key controls by area

Area Essential controls Cash and bank Limit who can sign or approve payments; require two approvals above a set amount; reconcile bank accounts monthly; reconcile daily takings; lock and review petty cash; check refunds Receivables Approve write-offs separately from collection; review the aged list monthly; have someone other than the bookkeeper open customer payments Payables Approve new suppliers before first payment; match every invoice to an order and delivery; watch for duplicate payments and unfamiliar suppliers Inventory Restrict access to stock; count stock regularly and investigate differences Payroll Check the payroll list against actual staff; approve overtime; separate who adds employees from who pays them General Compare results with budget monthly; protect and tag fixed assets; require mandatory leave so others cover each role; review expense claims

Segregation of duties

No single person should approve, record and pay a transaction. In a very small team, the founder should review and approve what one person records.

lessons.name: Warning signs to investigate & related concepts
lessons.description: Covers: Warning signs to investigate; Simple risk scoreboard; Look for the potholes ahead; Lead calmly through uncertainty; Be calm and realistically optimistic; Decide without all the facts; Business continuity checklist

payload.html:
Warning signs to investigate

an employee who never takes leave, lives beyond their means, resists sharing duties, or keeps records others cannot see; unexplained stock losses; customer complaints about payments not credited; missing documents.

Simple risk scoreboard

Rate each business function (cash, sales, purchasing, payroll, inventory, IT) on likelihood and impact of loss, from 1 (low) to 5 (high). Multiply the two. Tackle the highest scores first. Crisis readiness and business continuity Every business meets a crisis sooner or later: losing the biggest customer, a supply shock, a pandemic, a regional conflict. Small businesses are the most exposed because they have thin management and little cash. Prepare before it happens.

Look for the potholes ahead

Do you depend on too few customers or suppliers? What does your order pipeline look like for the next three months? Even a sharp recovery is dangerous: you must pay for stock before customers pay you.
Lead calmly through uncertainty

Be calm and realistically optimistic

Acknowledge what you do not know rather than overpromising. Use your team's know-how. Give people clear responsibility for specific issues instead of deciding everything yourself. Show empathy: staff are worried about their own income and families as well as the business. Communicate often and openly with staff, customers, suppliers and funders: what we know, what we don't know, and what we are doing.

Decide without all the facts

Waiting for complete information is an illusion. Work in a repeating cycle: decide, pause, assess the results, anticipate what comes next, act, and adjust as new information arrives.

Business continuity checklist

Name a small crisis team with clear owners for staff, operations and supply chain, customers, finance and digital. Stress-test your cash budget: what happens if revenue drops 30% or 50% for three months? List contractual obligations (rent, loans, tax, key supply contracts) and their impact under stress. Identify critical suppliers and line up alternatives; hold safety stock where it makes sense. Prepare for remote or flexible working, with secure access to files and systems. Agree in advance who speaks to staff, customers and the media, and what they will say. A crisis can also open opportunities, such as new products, channels or customers. Keep an eye out for them while you protect the core.

lessons.name: Reflect & apply
lessons.description: Questions to test yourself with, founder tips and the action checklist for this module.

payload.html:
Test your business against:

  • Could one person in my business take money without anyone else noticing? Who reconciles the bank account, and does anyone check their work? When did I last count stock or review payroll against real staff?

Practical advice from experience:

  • Prevention costs far less than investigation, and money lost to fraud is rarely recovered. Introduce controls as policy for everyone, not as a sign of distrust in anyone. Investigate every red flag promptly; ignored warning signs are how small frauds become large ones.

Before moving on, complete:

  • Set payment approval limits and dual sign-off above a threshold Reconcile every bank account monthly and have the founder review it Map who does what in cash, purchasing and payroll, and separate key duties Complete a risk scoreboard for each business function Write a short code of conduct covering conflicts of interest and gifts
